0001| #!/bin/sh
0002| # Forgel Code installer.
0003| #
0004| # One command installs the client into a per-user prefix:
0005| #
0006| #   curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgel-dev/code/v0.2.0/install.sh | sh
0007| #
0008| # The client goes into ${FORGEL_CODE_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share/forgel-code}, the
0009| # ``forgel-code`` launcher into ${FORGEL_CODE_BIN:-$HOME/.local/bin}, and that
0010| # directory is put on PATH through one marked block in the profile an
0011| # interactive login session of the login shell reads. The login shell is taken
0012| # from $SHELL, then from the invoking process (ps), then from the account login
0013| # shell; a shell outside the zsh and bash families gets the block in
0014| # $HOME/.profile and a warning that names the edited file. After writing the
0015| # block the installer starts that shell as a login interactive shell from a
0016| # cleared environment, in a process group of its own, under a hard time limit.
0017| # A watchdog stops that shell once the limit elapses, and the installer times
0018| # the check itself: a shell that outlived the limit fails the installation,
0019| # whatever the ordering of its own exit and the watchdog's timeout record. The
0020| # absence of a recorded timeout at the moment the check's result arrives is
0021| # never taken as evidence that the check kept its bound. Nothing the check
0022| # started outlives it: the dedicated group, and the descendants that left it,
0023| # are stopped on every exit path. The installer then checks that
0024| # ``forgel-code`` resolves to the launcher it just wrote. Re-running replaces
0025| # the installation; running with ``--uninstall`` removes it again.
0026| #
0027| # Environment variables:
0028| #   FORGEL_CODE_HOME            install prefix (default: $HOME/.local/share/forgel-code)
0029| #   FORGEL_CODE_BIN             launcher directory (default: $HOME/.local/bin)
0030| #   FORGEL_CODE_SOURCE          local checkout to install from, without network
0031| #   FORGEL_CODE_TAG             repository tag when no checkout is given (default: v0.2.0)
0032| #   FORGEL_CODE_REPOSITORY      repository URL used with FORGEL_CODE_TAG
0033| #   FORGEL_CODE_PYTHON          Python 3 interpreter (default: python3 on PATH)
0034| #   FORGEL_CODE_PROFILE         shell profile to edit (default: chosen from the login shell)
0035| #   FORGEL_CODE_NO_MODIFY_PATH  set to leave the shell profile untouched
0036| #   FORGEL_CODE_NO_PROFILE_EDIT the same opt-out under its older name
0037| #   FORGEL_CODE_TIMEOUT         seconds the fresh-shell check may take (default: 10)
0038| #
0039| # The script is POSIX ``sh`` and safe to pipe into: it never reads stdin.
0040|

0914| def _recording_login_shell(directory: Path, probe: Path, real_shell: str) -> Path:
0915|     """A handled shell name that records the check's directory, then runs ``real_shell``.
0916| 
0917|     ``ls -ld`` output of every ``forgel-code-check.*`` entry goes into ``probe``,
0918|     so the test can inspect the permissions of a directory that no longer exists
0919|     by the time the installer returns. The entries sit in the temporary tree of
0920|     the test, next to the checked shell's own ``$HOME``.
0921|     """
0922|     directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
0923|     stub = directory / "bash"
0924|     stub.write_text(
0925|         "#!/bin/sh\nprobe=%s\n" % _shell_quote(probe)
0926|         + 'ls -ld "$(dirname "$HOME")/tmp"/%s.* > "$probe/entries" 2>/dev/null || true\n'
0927|         % CHECK_PREFIX
0928|         + 'exec %s "$@"\n' % _shell_quote(real_shell),
0929|         encoding="utf-8",
0930|     )
0931|     stub.chmod(0o755)
0932|     return stub
0933|

0935| def _late_login_shell(directory: Path, launcher: Path) -> Path:
0936|     """A handled shell that answers past the bound but claims the launcher resolved.
0937| 
0938|     Its login session sleeps past a one-second bound and then prints exactly the
0939|     report a successful check prints. It ignores the graceful stop, so its own
0940|     exit, and not a signal, is what ends it.
0941|     """
0942|     directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
0943|     stub = directory / "bash"
0944|     stub.write_text(
0945|         "#!/bin/sh\n"
0946|         "trap '' TERM\n"
0947|         "sleep 2\n"
0948|         "printf 'forgel-fresh-path=%s\\n' '/usr/bin:/bin'\n"
0949|         "printf 'forgel-fresh-resolved=%s\\n' " + _shell_quote(launcher) + "\n"
0950|         "exit 0\n",
0951|         encoding="utf-8",
0952|     )
0953|     stub.chmod(0o755)
0954|     return stub
0955| 
0956| 
0957| def _late_login_shell_withholding_decision(directory: Path, launcher: Path) -> Path:
0958|     """A late shell that hides the watchdog's decision while it runs.
0959| 
0960|     It removes the write permission of the private check directory, so the
0961|     watchdog cannot record whether the bound elapsed, and restores it when it
0962|     exits past the bound, still printing the report of a successful check. The
0963|     directory is found the way the permission probe finds it: under the TMPDIR
0964|     the installer was given, next to the checked shell's own ``$HOME``.
0965|     """
0966|     directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
0967|     stub = directory / "bash"
0968|     stub.write_text(
0969|         "#!/bin/sh\n"
0970|         "trap '' TERM\n"
0971|         "check_dir=\n"
0972|         'for candidate in "$(dirname "$HOME")/tmp"/%s.*; do\n' % CHECK_PREFIX
0973|         + '    [ -d "$candidate" ] || continue\n'
0974|         + "    check_dir=$candidate\n"
0975|         + '    chmod 500 "$candidate" 2>/dev/null || true\n'
0976|         + "done\n"
0977|         + "sleep 2\n"
0978|         + "printf 'forgel-fresh-path=%s\\n' '/usr/bin:/bin'\n"
0979|         + "printf 'forgel-fresh-resolved=%s\\n' " + _shell_quote(launcher) + "\n"
0980|         + 'if [ -n "$check_dir" ]; then\n'
0981|         + '    chmod 700 "$check_dir" 2>/dev/null || true\n'
0982|         + "fi\n"
0983|         + "exit 0\n",
0984|         encoding="utf-8",
0985|     )
0986|     stub.chmod(0o755)
0987|     return stub

0001| # code
0002| 
0003| Forgel Code — thin console client for Forgel over the engine's machine-readable
0004| commands.
0005| 
0006| The client does not import the engine. Its only channel is running
0007| `forgel <command> --json` as a separate process and reading exactly one JSON
0008| object from stdout. The model, sandbox, independent QA, review and release
0009| approval stay in the engine: the client never calls a model, never reads
0010| project files and never runs checks itself.
0011| 
0012| ## Install
0013| 
0014| Forgel Code installs with one command. It needs Python 3.9 or newer with the
0015| `pip` module it ships, and the `forgel` engine on `PATH`.
0016| 
0017| ```sh
0018| curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgel-dev/code/v0.2.0/install.sh | sh
0019| ```
0020| 
0021| The installer puts the client into `~/.local/share/forgel-code` and a
0022| `forgel-code` launcher into `~/.local/bin`, then adds that directory to `PATH`
0023| through one marked block in the profile your login shell reads. No virtual
0024| environment and no activation step are involved, and the same command run again
0025| replaces the installation instead of duplicating anything.
0026| 
0027| | Login shell | Profile file that receives the block |
0028| | --- | --- |
0029| | zsh | `~/.zshrc` |
0030| | bash | the first existing of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.profile`; `~/.bash_profile` is created when none of them exists |
0031| | other POSIX `sh` | `~/.profile`, with a warning on stderr that names the file and the detected shell |
0032| 
0033| The login shell comes from `$SHELL`. When that is unset, empty or names a shell
0034| the installer does not handle, it reads the shell of the invoking process and
0035| then the account login shell — the macOS Directory Service entry, otherwise the
0036| passwd entry — and only then falls back to `~/.profile`. The block is never
0037| written to `~/.bashrc` alone, because a login bash shell does not read that
0038| file. A profile file that does not exist yet is created.
0039| 
0040| The block carries a `case "$PATH:"` guard and prepends the launcher directory
0041| only when it is not already there, so sourcing it again, or sourcing several
0042| profiles that carry it, leaves exactly one entry. There is no unguarded
0043| `export PATH=...` line.
0044| 
0045| After writing the block the installer checks it: it starts the detected login
0046| shell as a login interactive shell from a cleared environment, under a bounded
0047| time limit enforced without GNU `timeout`, and requires `command -v forgel-code`
0048| to resolve to the launcher it just wrote. On success it prints the detected
0049| shell, the edited profile file and the path that fresh shell resolved. If the
0050| check fails, or the shell does not answer within the limit, it exits non-zero
0051| and prints on stderr the edited profile file, the exact block it wrote, the
0052| shell it checked, the `PATH` that shell saw and what `forgel-code` resolved to,
0053| so a profile your login shell never reads is never reported as active.
0054| Re-running keeps exactly one marked block and leaves the rest of the file as it
0055| was.
0056| 
0057| The client has no dependencies and builds through the small in-tree PEP 517
0058| backend (`_build_backend.py`), so the installer never needs a package index.
0059| Editable installs are not supported: the backend implements only the
0060| `build_wheel` and `build_sdist` hooks.
0061| 
0062| ### Options
0063| 
0064| | Variable | Effect |
0065| | --- | --- |
0066| | `FORGEL_CODE_HOME` | installation prefix (default `~/.local/share/forgel-code`) |
0067| | `FORGEL_CODE_BIN` | directory of the `forgel-code` launcher (default `~/.local/bin`) |
0068| | `FORGEL_CODE_PROFILE` | shell profile that receives the `PATH` block, instead of the detected one; the uninstall cleans it too |
0069| | `FORGEL_CODE_NO_MODIFY_PATH` | set it to leave the shell profile untouched |
0070| | `FORGEL_CODE_SOURCE` | install from a local checkout instead of the network |
0071| 
0072| With `FORGEL_CODE_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1` no profile file is opened for writing, no
0073| fresh-shell check runs, the installer prints the exact line to add yourself and
0074| exits with code 0.
0075| 
0076| ```sh
0077| export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
0078| ```
0079| 
0080| ```sh
0081| FORGEL_CODE_SOURCE=/path/to/code sh install.sh
0082| ```
0083| 
0084| The `forgel` engine must be available on `PATH`; use `--engine PATH` or
0085| `$FORGEL_ENGINE` to point at a specific binary. `forgel-code --version` prints
0086| the installed version.
0087| 
0088| ### Update
0089| 
0090| ```sh
0091| curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgel-dev/code/v0.2.0/install.sh | sh
0092| ```
0093| 
0094| ### Uninstall
0095| 
0096| ```sh
0097| curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgel-dev/code/v0.2.0/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall
0098| ```
0099| 
0100| The uninstall removes the installation prefix, the `forgel-code` launcher and
0101| the marked `PATH` block from every profile file this installer can have written:
0102| `~/.zshrc`, `~/.zprofile`, `~/.zshenv`, `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`,
0103| `~/.profile` and `~/.bashrc`. When `FORGEL_CODE_PROFILE` names another file, the
0104| same run also removes the marked block from that exact file, so a block left
0105| behind by an install that edited a custom profile — including an install that
0106| wrote the block and then failed its fresh-shell check — does not survive. A file
0107| that is missing or carries no marker is left alone, no file is created, and the
0108| rest of each edited file is left unchanged.
0109| 
0110| Windows is not the main installation method; the fallback there is `python -m pip install --user` of the pinned revision.
0111| 
0112| ## Interactive session
0113| 
0114| Starting `forgel-code` with no arguments opens an interactive session instead of
0115| printing usage text. It shows a prompt and stays open until you leave, so you
0116| work by writing sentences rather than by translating every intent into a
0117| command.
0118| 
0119| Each sentence is handed to the engine's project agent as one free-form request
0120| and the agent's answer is shown in the session. The session also shows the
0121| project it is working on, and re-reads the task and release state from the
0122| engine on its own, so progress becomes visible without asking for a status
0123| again.
0124| 
0125| Some sentences ask the session for one specific action:
0126| 
0127| | You write | What the session asks the engine for |
0128| | --- | --- |
0129| | a plain sentence | the project agent's answer |
0130| | `plan <goal>` | a plan for the goal, shown with its tasks in plan order and their states |
0131| | `accept <task>` | accepting that task |
0132| | `rework <task> <remarks>` | sending that task back with the remarks |
0133| | `retry <task>` | retrying that task |
0134| | `pause` | pausing work |
0135| | `resume` | resuming work |
0136| | `switch to <key>` | selecting another project; every later request and every later state shown uses the new project |
0137| | `leave`, `exit`, `quit`, or the end of the input | ending the session |
0138| 
0139| A sentence that names no action, or more than one, gets a clarification and
0140| nothing is carried out. A request that becomes a plan shows its tasks in plan
0141| order, and one that becomes a task shows that task with its title and state.
0142| When an engine call fails, the session shows the reason and the next possible
0143| step and stays usable for the next request; leaving after a failure needs no
0144| restart. Replies follow the language of your message.
0145| 
0146| Adopting a repository, creating a project, setting or changing a secret and
0147| changing configuration are not part of the conversation. A sentence never
0148| carries them out; the session only points you to the explicit command for them.
0149| 
0150| Leaving ends the session at once: the client sends nothing further to the
0151| engine and keeps no transcript. Key material never reaches the screen, because
0152| a value that names a secret is replaced before it is shown.
0153| 
0154| The interactive session adds no capability of its own: every answer and every
0155| piece of state comes from the engine, and the client still calls no model, reads
0156| no project and runs no check. All commands below keep working one-shot, with the
0157| same output, exit status and `--json` form as before.
0158| 
0159| ## Commands
0160| 
0161| Every client command is a thin wrapper over an existing engine command, and
0162| the engine is always called with `--json`. `<key>` below is the project the
0163| client session selected with `forgel-code use`; while nothing is selected the
0164| client passes no `--project` and the engine keeps its own active project.
0165| 
0166| | Client command | Engine command | Purpose |
0167| | --- | --- | --- |
0168| | `forgel-code say <phrase>` | `forgel say "<phrase>"` | Turn a free phrase into a task |
0169| | `forgel-code status` | `forgel status` | State of the task and the milestone |
0170| | `forgel-code tasks` | `forgel tasks` | List tasks |
0171| | `forgel-code task <task>` | `forgel tasks` | State of one task, picked out of the engine's task list |
0172| | `forgel-code accept <task>` | `forgel task accept --task <task> [--project <key>]` | Accept a task |
0173| | `forgel-code rework <task> <remark...>` | `forgel task reject --task <task> --notes "<remark>" [--project <key>]` | Send a task back for rework with remarks |
0174| | `forgel-code resume` | `forgel resume` | Start or resume work |
0175| | `forgel-code pause` | `forgel pause` | Pause work |
0176| | `forgel-code plan "<goal>" [--milestone <key>]` | `forgel plan [<key>] --goal "<goal>"` | Decompose the milestone goal into tasks |
0177| | `forgel-code history` | `forgel history` | Short session history |
0178| | `forgel-code projects` | `forgel projects` | List projects |
0179| | `forgel-code session` | `forgel session` | Show the session the engine reports |
0180| | `forgel-code use <key>` | `forgel use <key>` | Select the active project |
0181| 
0182| `forgel-code` does not read a project itself: `task <task>` asks the engine for
0183| its task list and shows the one task you named. If that task is not in the
0184| engine's answer — or appears there more than once — the client reports it and
0185| exits with a non-zero code.
0186| 
0187| `accept` and `rework` lean on the engine's `task` command and its positional
0188| actions: accepting is `task accept`, sending back is `task reject`, and the
0189| remarks travel in the engine's `--notes`. The client adds no subcommand and no
0190| option of its own. The exact engine calls behind them are:
0191| 
0192| ```sh
0193| forgel task accept --task <task> --json
0194| forgel task reject --task <task> --notes "<remark>" --json
0195| ```
0196| 
0197| When the running engine does not provide the action a point needs, the client
0198| prints the engine's own message plus an explicit note ("no engine command for
0199| this point") and exits with a non-zero code instead of inventing behaviour.
0200| That decision is taken from the engine's return code and structured error
0201| fields, never from the wording of its message, so it does not depend on the
0202| locale.
0203| 
0204| ### Output
0205| 
0206| Without a flag a command prints human readable text. With `--json` it prints
0207| exactly one JSON object to stdout:
0208| 
0209| ```json
0210| {"command": "status", "project": "acme", "ok": true, "result": {}}
0211| ```
0212| 
0213| The `project` field is the project key actually handed to the engine, or `null`
0214| when nothing was passed. On failure — including an argument-parse error — the
0215| client exits with a non-zero code and, with `--json`, prints one JSON object
0216| with `"ok": false` and the message under `error`. A structured engine refusal
0217| (`"ok": false` in the engine's answer) is a failure even when the engine exits
0218| with code 0, and its own fields are carried through. A failure report names the
0219| engine that answered: the path configured by `--engine`, `$FORGEL_ENGINE` or
0220| `forgel` leads the message.
0221| 
0222| ### Active project
0223| 
0224| `forgel-code use <key>` hands the key to the engine and, only when the engine
0225| accepts it, makes it the active project; every project-scoped command then
0226| passes `--project <key>`. `forgel-code projects` lists what the engine knows
0227| about. Until you pick a key no `--project` argument is sent, so the engine's own
0228| active project is used. Set `FORGEL_CODE_HOME` to move the session file.
0229| 
0230| ### Timeout
0231| 
0232| The engine call is bounded. `--timeout SECONDS` sets the limit for one call,
0233| `$FORGEL_CODE_TIMEOUT` sets it for the environment, and the default is 600
0234| seconds. When the limit elapses the client kills the engine and fails with a
0235| structured error instead of blocking. The engine's stdout is always decoded as
0236| UTF-8 and the child process does not receive the client's stdin.
0237| 
0238| `--json`, `--engine` and `--timeout` are parsed as options of their own and are
0239| never substituted inside argument text, so a phrase or remark that mentions
0240| such a word reaches the engine unchanged. Put `--` before a remark that itself
0241| begins with a hyphen.
0242| 
0243| ## Tests
0244| 
0245| From a checkout the suite needs nothing but the Python standard library and no
0246| network access:
0247| 
0248| ```sh
0249| python -m unittest discover -s tests
0250| ```
0251| 
0252| That command runs the whole suite — no environment variable, marker or default
0253| option leaves a test out — and it covers the installer scenarios too, which run
0254| the real `install.sh` with a real install through `pip` into a temporary home
0255| directory and a real detected login shell.
0256| 
0257| Installing the client with its `test` extra brings the pytest the wheel
0258| declares, so a pinned revision can run the same suite too:
0259| 
0260| ```sh
0261| python3 -m pip install "https://github.com/forgel-dev/code/archive/refs/tags/v0.1.1.tar.gz[test]"
0262| python -m pytest -q
0263| ```

0001| """The timeout verdict follows the check's own duration, not a recorded marker.
0002| 
0003| A checked step that runs past the configured bound and exits on its own before
0004| the watchdog has recorded a timeout must still fail: the installer times the
0005| check itself, so the absence of a recorded timeout at the moment the result
0006| becomes available is never evidence that the step kept its bound. That verdict
0007| holds for a step that ends just after the bound, at it, or well past it. The
0008| clock the check is timed with is a stub, so the moment the step ends relative to
0009| the bound is forced explicitly and nothing waits for real time to pass.
0010| """

0032| # The fabricated clock the installer is handed: the nanoseconds since the epoch
0033| # it answers for the check's start, and the distance to the answer it gives for
0034| # the check's result. The distances are expressed against the one-second bound
0035| # under test: three times the bound has provably overrun it, one millisecond
0036| # over it ends just after it, and a zero distance keeps the step well inside it.
0037| CLOCK_BASE_NS = 1700000000000000000
0038| CLOCK_OVERRUN_NS = 3000000000
0039| CLOCK_JUST_AFTER_NS = 1001000000

0043| # The stand-in for the clock the check is timed with, exactly as the external
0044| # dependency records it: ``date +%s%N`` answers a timestamp, so the stub answers
0045| # a timestamp too. It advances by FORGEL_STUB_CLOCK_STEP nanoseconds and counts
0046| # its invocations in FORGEL_STUB_CLOCK_COUNTER, so the distance between the
0047| # check's start and its result is fixed by the test and not by real time.
0048| CLOCK_STUB = """#!/bin/sh
0049| # Deterministic stand-in for `date +%s%N`.
0050| # Answers FORGEL_STUB_CLOCK_BASE plus one FORGEL_STUB_CLOCK_STEP per call.
0051| counter=$FORGEL_STUB_CLOCK_COUNTER
0052| call=0
0053| if [ -r "$counter" ]; then
0054|     call=$(cat "$counter" 2>/dev/null) || call=0
0055| fi
0056| case $call in
0057|     ''|*[!0-9]*) call=0 ;;
0058| esac
0059| call=$((call + 1))
0060| printf '%s\\n' "$call" > "$counter" 2>/dev/null || true
0061| printf '%s\\n' "$((FORGEL_STUB_CLOCK_BASE + (call - 1) * FORGEL_STUB_CLOCK_STEP))"

0001| # Changelog
0002| 
0003| All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.
0004| 
0005| The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/),
0006| and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).
0007| 
0008| ## [Unreleased]
0009| 
0010| ### Added
0011| 
0012| - Open an interactive session when the client starts with no arguments — `forgel-code` now shows a prompt and stays open instead of printing usage text. A sentence typed at the prompt is handed to the engine's project agent as one free-form request and the agent's answer is shown in the session. The session shows the selected project and lets the owner switch it without leaving, shows a plan as its ordered tasks with their states and a new task with its title and state, and re-reads the task and release state from the engine on its own so progress appears without asking for a status. Accepting a task, sending it back with remarks, retrying a failed task, pausing and resuming work are asked for in plain language, an ambiguous or unmatched request gets a clarification and performs nothing, a failure shows the reason and the next possible step while the session stays usable, and replies follow the language of the owner's message. Adopting a repository, creating a project, secrets and configuration stay explicit separate actions that a sentence never triggers, key material never reaches the screen, and leaving — or the end of the input — ends the session at once. The session adds no capability: every answer and every piece of state still comes from the engine, and every one-shot usage keeps its previous output, exit status and `--json` form.
0013| 
0014| ### Changed
0015| 
0016| - Speed up the suite without weakening a test — the expensive duplicated work is gone instead of a scenario: one read-only checkout copy and one prepared installation per scenario group are shared by the tests that only read them, and the bounded-check cases configure a limit below the product default.
0017| - Remove every statement of a suite completion time, duration or runtime bound from the documentation — the README `## Tests` section still says that one documented command runs the whole suite, that the installer situations are covered by a real installation into a throwaway home location with a real detected login shell, and that a run from a source checkout needs only the Python standard library and no network access, but it no longer promises how long such a run takes.
0018| 
0019| ### Fixed
0020| 
0021| - Refuse a free-text request to create or change key material, to change configuration and to create or scaffold a project in English and in Russian, including their bare wording — a sentence that names a key without any credential term, the configuration without the word `configuration`, or a project that is scaffolded rather than created is now recognised, refused in the session and never forwarded to the engine, and the refusal states that the action needs the explicit operation and names the client's own `forgel-code` command to use. Ordinary conversation that merely mentions a key, the configuration or a project still reaches the engine unchanged, and every refusal that already existed keeps its wording.
0022| - Mask the value of the French password label when it is written with underscores or hyphens — the label is now recognised as a secret label in its joined spellings as well as its spaced one, in any letter case, so an engine reply or error that carries it next to a value is redacted before display and before retention. Every value form already handled for the spaced label is covered, a joined label without an adjacent value leaves the message unchanged, and every other supported label in every language redacts exactly as before.
0023| - Refuse sensitive explicit actions phrased in French and Spanish as well as in English and Russian — a free-text request to create a project, to set or define a credential such as a password, a token or a key, or to change configuration or settings is recognised in all four languages the session speaks, in either word order, in ordinary inflections and with or without diacritics. The refusal-and-redirect answer speaks the language of the message, states that such an action is never carried out from a sentence, and then points at the client's own explicit command `forgel-code` together with the action it performs — creating a project, setting or defining a password, a token or a key, or changing the configuration — in the same style as the English and Russian refusals. Nothing of the refused request is sent onward, ordinary French and Spanish conversation still reaches the engine unchanged, and English and Russian results stay exactly as they were.
0024| - Mask the credential of a label followed by an ordinary descriptor word — a secret label followed by a word such as `value`, `field` or `string` used to hide that descriptor and leave the credential itself on screen and in the retained state; the descriptor now stays readable and the value, including the one behind a copula or a separator, is replaced by the existing masking placeholder. Sentences that only mention a secret word are still shown unchanged.
0025| - Remove the PATH block from the profile named by `FORGEL_CODE_PROFILE` — `--uninstall` again cleans the marked block out of the profile the override variable names, in addition to the six standard profile files, so a block left by a completed install or by an install that failed its fresh-shell check no longer survives.
0026| - Point the README install, update and uninstall commands at the current `v0.1.1` release installer — the documented commands no longer fetch the stale install script, all three name one and the same install-script URL, and the guard in `tests/test_readme_install.py` fails the suite when any of them carries an older tag or a divergent install-script URL.

0002| # Forgel Code installer.
0003| #
0004| # One command installs the client into a per-user prefix:
0005| #
0006| #   curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgel-dev/code/v0.2.0/install.sh | sh
0007| #
0008| # The client goes into ${FORGEL_CODE_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share/forgel-code}, the
0009| # ``forgel-code`` launcher into ${FORGEL_CODE_BIN:-$HOME/.local/bin}, and that
0010| # directory is put on PATH through one marked block in the profile an
0011| # interactive login session of the login shell reads. The login shell is taken
0012| # from $SHELL, then from the invoking process (ps), then from the account login
0013| # shell; a shell outside the zsh and bash families gets the block in
0014| # $HOME/.profile and a warning that names the edited file. After writing the
0015| # block the installer starts that shell as a login interactive shell from a
0016| # cleared environment, in a process group of its own, under a hard time limit.
0017| # A watchdog stops that shell once the limit elapses, and the installer times
0018| # the check itself: a shell that outlived the limit fails the installation,
0019| # whatever the ordering of its own exit and the watchdog's timeout record. The
0020| # absence of a recorded timeout at the moment the check's result arrives is
0021| # never taken as evidence that the check kept its bound. Nothing the check
0022| # started outlives it: the dedicated group, and the descendants that left it,
0023| # are stopped on every exit path. The installer then checks that
0024| # ``forgel-code`` resolves to the launcher it just wrote. Re-running replaces
0025| # the installation; running with ``--uninstall`` removes it again.
0026| #
0027| # Installing the client alone is not enough to use it, so the same run also
0028| # makes sure an engine the client supports is in place. It asks the engine's own
0029| # installer which version the configured engine source provides, without
0030| # installing anything, and reads the version of an engine that is already
0031| # present. Only then does it decide: an available engine is installed when none
0032| # is present, the present engine is kept when the available one is not newer and
0033| # the present one is supported, a strictly newer available engine replaces the
0034| # present one, and anything else ends the run as a failure that names the
0035| # required minimum, the version found and the action the user can take. A
0036| # successful run always states the engine version in place and how it was
0037| # obtained. ``--client-only`` installs the client alone and touches no engine.
0038| # Reading a version report, and installing a version, are the engine installer's
0039| # own jobs; this script only decides and delegates.
0040| #
0041| # Environment variables:
0042| #   FORGEL_CODE_HOME            install prefix (default: $HOME/.local/share/forgel-code)
0043| #   FORGEL_CODE_BIN             launcher directory (default: $HOME/.local/bin)
0044| #   FORGEL_CODE_SOURCE          local checkout to install from, without network
0045| #   FORGEL_CODE_TAG             repository tag when no checkout is given (default: v0.2.0)
0046| #   FORGEL_CODE_REPOSITORY      repository URL used with FORGEL_CODE_TAG

0643|                     pid = ids[j]

0647|                         count++

0655| # Start the checked command in a process group of its own, and record that group
0656| # for the whole lifetime of the check: the command may exit at once while
0657| # something it started lives on in the same group. The launcher puts itself in a
0658| # new session, and so in a new process group, before it runs the command; the
0659| # group id is therefore its own pid. Python is already required to install the
0660| # client. A shell without it falls back to its own job control, and otherwise to
0661| # the descendant sweep alone.

0668| try:
0669|     os.setsid()
0670| except OSError:
0671|     try:
0672|         os.setpgid(0, 0)
0673|     except OSError:
0674|         pass

0676|     os.execvp(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[1:])

0683|     fi

0690| # Signal every member of a process group. The caller's own group is never
0691| # signalled, so a check that could not be placed in a group of its own cannot
0692| # make the cleanup reach the installer itself.
0693| signal_group() {
0694|     signal=$1
0695|     group=$2
0696|     case $group in
0697|         ''|*[!0-9]*) return 0 ;;
0698|     esac
0699|     own=
0700|     if command -v ps >/dev/null 2>&1; then
0701|         own=$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ') || own=
0702|     fi
0703|     if [ -n "$own" ] && [ "$group" = "$own" ]; then
0704|         return 0
0705|     fi
0706|     if kill -"$signal" "-$group" 2>/dev/null; then
0707|         return 0
0708|     fi
0709|     # A shell that cannot name a group signals its members one by one.
0710|     for pid in $(process_group "$group"); do
0711|         kill -"$signal" "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true
0712|     done
0713|     return 0
0714| }

0716| # Stop what the checked command started. The dedicated process group is the
0717| # primary target: everything that stayed in it goes at once, on the success path
0718| # as well as on the timeout path. A sweep of the checked command's descendants
0719| # follows, so a descendant that left the group is reached as well.
0720| stop_check() {

0723|     if [ -n "$CHECK_CHILD" ]; then

0726|         done
0727|         kill -"$signal" "$CHECK_CHILD" 2>/dev/null || true

0732| # Release everything the bounded check owns: the watchdog, the checked process

0736| # release reads is cleared only after it has been used.
0737| cleanup_check() {

0739|         return 0
0740|     fi

0744|         wait "$CHECK_WATCHER" 2>/dev/null || true

0746|     fi

0748|         stop_check KILL
0749|         if [ -n "$CHECK_CHILD" ]; then
0750|             wait "$CHECK_CHILD" 2>/dev/null || true
0751|         fi
0752|         CHECK_GROUP=
0753|         CHECK_CHILD=
0754|     fi

0767| # Wait, for a bounded moment, until the watchdog has recorded its decision in
0768| # the private check directory: ``timed-out`` when the bound had elapsed before
0769| # the checked command exited, ``finished`` when it saw the command gone first.
0770| # Status 0 means the decision is there, 1 that the watchdog did not answer
0771| # within DECISION_WAIT seconds. The decision says which stop to expect; it is
0772| # not the verdict, which is the time the check took (see ``bounded_run``). The
0773| # wait never depends on the checked command, so a watchdog that never answers
0774| # delays the installer by that fixed limit at most.
0775| await_decision() {
0776|     decision_dir=$1
0777|     waited=0
0778|     while :; do
0779|         if [ -e "$decision_dir/timed-out" ] || [ -e "$decision_dir/finished" ]; then
0780|             return 0
0781|         fi
0782|         if [ "$waited" -ge "$DECISION_WAIT" ]; then
0783|             return 1
0784|         fi
0785|         sleep 1 2>/dev/null || true

0787|     done

0790| # Run a command under a hard time bound. ``timeout`` from GNU coreutils is not
0791| # required and is not used: the command runs in the background and a watchdog
0792| # stops it once the bound elapsed. The watchdog records ``timed-out`` in the
0793| # private directory before it starts the graceful stop, and ``finished`` when it
0794| # saw the command gone before the bound; that record says which stop to expect,
0795| # never what the verdict is. The installer times the check itself and reports a
0796| # timeout whenever the measured time reached the bound, so the ordering between
0797| # the command's own exit, the record and the read of the result cannot turn a
0798| # step that overran into a success. A command that finished inside the bound
0799| # keeps its own status, a nonzero one included. After the graceful stop the
0800| # watchdog forcefully stops the rest of the checked command's process group once
0801| # the grace period has passed. Nothing the function starts survives it.
0802| # CHECK_STATUS is 124 when the bound elapsed.
0803| #
0804| # The checked command leads a process group of its own (see ``start_check``), so
0805| # the group is what the cleanup signals, on the success path as much as on the
0806| # timeout path. Its three standard descriptors are redirected, so the group has
0807| # no terminal to hold it and cannot stop on a terminal access.
0808| bounded_run() {
0809|     limit=$1
0810|     shift
0811|     CHECK_STATUS=0
0812|     CHECK_OUTPUT=
0813|     CHECK_CLEANED=
0814|     CHECK_CHILD=
0815|     CHECK_GROUP=
0816|     if ! create_check_dir; then
0817|         return 1
0818|     fi
0819|     out=$CHECK_DIR/output
0820|     timed_out=$CHECK_DIR/timed-out
0821|     finished=$CHECK_DIR/finished
0822|     saved_umask=$(umask)
0823|     umask 077
0824|     if ! : > "$out"; then
0825|         umask "$saved_umask"
0826|         cleanup_check
0827|         return 1
0828|     fi
0829|     started=$(now_millis)
0830|     start_check "$out" "$@"
0831|     umask "$saved_umask"
0832|     child=$CHECK_CHILD
0833|     (
0834|         exec > /dev/null 2>&1 < /dev/null
0835|         sleeper=
0836|         trap 'kill "$sleeper" 2>/dev/null || true; exit 0' TERM
0837|         elapsed=0
0838|         while [ "$elapsed" -lt "$limit" ]; do
0839|             sleep 1 &
0840|             sleeper=$!
0841|             wait "$sleeper" 2>/dev/null || true
0842|             sleeper=
0843|             elapsed=$((elapsed + 1))
0844|             if ! kill -0 "$child" 2>/dev/null; then
0845|                 # The command was gone inside the bound; record that so the
0846|                 # caller knows which stop to expect.
0847|                 : > "$finished" 2>/dev/null || true
0848|                 exit 0
0849|             fi
0850|         done
0851|         : > "$timed_out" 2>/dev/null || true
0852|         stop_check TERM
0853|         sleep "$VERIFY_GRACE" 2>/dev/null || true
0854|         stop_check KILL
0855|     ) &
0856|     CHECK_WATCHER=$!
0857|     wait "$child" || CHECK_STATUS=$?
0858|     ended=$(now_millis)
0859|     measured=$((ended - started))
0860|     if await_decision "$CHECK_DIR"; then
0861|         # The watchdog records its decision before it stops anything, so on
0862|         # the timeout path it may still own the graceful then the forceful
0863|         # stop; let it finish so nothing outlives the check.
0864|         wait "$CHECK_WATCHER" 2>/dev/null || true
0865|     else
0866|         # A watchdog that never answers is not allowed to hold the installer. A
0867|         # decision that never arrives is not evidence that the bound was kept;
0868|         # the measured time decides that below.
0869|         kill -KILL "$CHECK_WATCHER" 2>/dev/null || true
0870|         wait "$CHECK_WATCHER" 2>/dev/null || true
0871|     fi
0872|     # The verdict is the time the check took, never the presence of a record: a
0873|     # step that outlived the bound is a timeout even when it exited on its own
0874|     # before the timeout was recorded, and a step inside the bound keeps its own
0875|     # status, a nonzero one included.
0876|     if [ -e "$timed_out" ] || [ "$measured" -ge "$((limit * 1000))" ]; then
0877|         CHECK_STATUS=124
0878|     fi
0879|     CHECK_OUTPUT=$(cat "$out") || CHECK_OUTPUT=
0880|     # The check is released here, before any state the release reads is
0881|     # cleared: a successful check leaves nothing behind, exactly like a failed
0882|     # or a timed-out one.
0883|     cleanup_check
0884|     return 0
0885| }

0001| # code
0002| 
0003| Forgel Code — thin console client for Forgel over the engine's machine-readable
0004| commands.
0005| 
0006| The client does not import the engine. Its only channel is running
0007| `forgel <command> --json` as a separate process and reading exactly one JSON
0008| object from stdout. The model, sandbox, independent QA, review and release
0009| approval stay in the engine: the client never calls a model, never reads
0010| project files and never runs checks itself.
0011| 
0012| ## Install
0013| 
0014| Forgel Code installs with one command. It needs Python 3.9 or newer with the
0015| `pip` module it ships, and the `forgel` engine on `PATH`.
0016| 
0017| ```sh
0018| curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgel-dev/code/v0.2.0/install.sh | sh
0019| ```
0020| 
0021| The installer puts the client into `~/.local/share/forgel-code` and a
0022| `forgel-code` launcher into `~/.local/bin`, then adds that directory to `PATH`
0023| through one marked block in the profile your login shell reads. No virtual
0024| environment and no activation step are involved, and the same command run again
0025| replaces the installation instead of duplicating anything.
0026| 
0027| | Login shell | Profile file that receives the block |
0028| | --- | --- |
0029| | zsh | `~/.zshrc` |
0030| | bash | the first existing of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.profile`; `~/.bash_profile` is created when none of them exists |
0031| | other POSIX `sh` | `~/.profile`, with a warning on stderr that names the file and the detected shell |
0032| 
0033| The login shell comes from `$SHELL`. When that is unset, empty or names a shell
0034| the installer does not handle, it reads the shell of the invoking process and
0035| then the account login shell — the macOS Directory Service entry, otherwise the
0036| passwd entry — and only then falls back to `~/.profile`. The block is never
0037| written to `~/.bashrc` alone, because a login bash shell does not read that
0038| file. A profile file that does not exist yet is created.
0039| 
0040| The block carries a `case "$PATH:"` guard and prepends the launcher directory
0041| only when it is not already there, so sourcing it again, or sourcing several
0042| profiles that carry it, leaves exactly one entry. There is no unguarded
0043| `export PATH=...` line.
0044| 
0045| After writing the block the installer checks it: it starts the detected login
0046| shell as a login interactive shell from a cleared environment, under a bounded
0047| time limit enforced without GNU `timeout`, and requires `command -v forgel-code`
0048| to resolve to the launcher it just wrote. On success it prints the detected
0049| shell, the edited profile file and the path that fresh shell resolved. If the
0050| check fails, or the shell does not answer within the limit, it exits non-zero
0051| and prints on stderr the edited profile file, the exact block it wrote, the
0052| shell it checked, the `PATH` that shell saw and what `forgel-code` resolved to,
0053| so a profile your login shell never reads is never reported as active.
0054| Re-running keeps exactly one marked block and leaves the rest of the file as it
0055| was.
0056| 
0057| The client has no dependencies and builds through the small in-tree PEP 517
0058| backend (`_build_backend.py`), so the installer never needs a package index.
0059| Editable installs are not supported: the backend implements only the
0060| `build_wheel` and `build_sdist` hooks.
0061| 
0062| ### Options
0063| 
0064| | Variable | Effect |
0065| | --- | --- |
0066| | `FORGEL_CODE_HOME` | installation prefix (default `~/.local/share/forgel-code`) |
0067| | `FORGEL_CODE_BIN` | directory of the `forgel-code` launcher (default `~/.local/bin`) |
0068| | `FORGEL_CODE_PROFILE` | shell profile that receives the `PATH` block, instead of the detected one; the uninstall cleans it too |
0069| | `FORGEL_CODE_NO_MODIFY_PATH` | set it to leave the shell profile untouched |
0070| | `FORGEL_CODE_SOURCE` | install from a local checkout instead of the network |
0071| 
0072| With `FORGEL_CODE_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1` no profile file is opened for writing, no
0073| fresh-shell check runs, the installer prints the exact line to add yourself and
0074| exits with code 0.
0075| 
0076| ```sh
0077| export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
0078| ```
0079| 
0080| ```sh
0081| FORGEL_CODE_SOURCE=/path/to/code sh install.sh
0082| ```
0083| 
0084| The `forgel` engine must be available on `PATH`; use `--engine PATH` or
0085| `$FORGEL_ENGINE` to point at a specific binary. `forgel-code --version` prints
0086| the installed version.
0087| 
0088| ### Update
0089| 
0090| ```sh
0091| curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgel-dev/code/v0.2.0/install.sh | sh
0092| ```
0093| 
0094| ### Uninstall
0095| 
0096| ```sh
0097| curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgel-dev/code/v0.2.0/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall
0098| ```
0099| 
0100| The uninstall removes the installation prefix, the `forgel-code` launcher and
0101| the marked `PATH` block from every profile file this installer can have written:
0102| `~/.zshrc`, `~/.zprofile`, `~/.zshenv`, `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`,
0103| `~/.profile` and `~/.bashrc`. When `FORGEL_CODE_PROFILE` names another file, the
0104| same run also removes the marked block from that exact file, so a block left
0105| behind by an install that edited a custom profile — including an install that
0106| wrote the block and then failed its fresh-shell check — does not survive. A file
0107| that is missing or carries no marker is left alone, no file is created, and the
0108| rest of each edited file is left unchanged.
0109| 
0110| Windows is not the main installation method; the fallback there is `python -m pip install --user` of the pinned revision.
0111| 
0112| ## Interactive session
0113| 
0114| Starting `forgel-code` with no arguments opens an interactive session instead of
0115| printing usage text. It shows a prompt and stays open until you leave, so you
0116| work by writing sentences rather than by translating every intent into a
0117| command.
0118|

0006| #   curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgel-dev/code/v0.2.0/install.sh | sh
0007| #
0008| # The client goes into ${FORGEL_CODE_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share/forgel-code}, the
0009| # ``forgel-code`` launcher into ${FORGEL_CODE_BIN:-$HOME/.local/bin}, and that
0010| # directory is put on PATH through one marked block in the profile an
0011| # interactive login session of the login shell reads. The login shell is taken
0012| # from $SHELL, then from the invoking process (ps), then from the account login
0013| # shell; a shell outside the zsh and bash families gets the block in
0014| # $HOME/.profile and a warning that names the edited file. After writing the
0015| # block the installer starts that shell as a login interactive shell from a
0016| # cleared environment, in a process group of its own, under a hard time limit.
0017| # A watchdog stops that shell once the limit elapses, and the installer times
0018| # the check itself: a shell that outlived the limit fails the installation,
0019| # whatever the ordering of its own exit and the watchdog's timeout record. The
0020| # absence of a recorded timeout at the moment the check's result arrives is
0021| # never taken as evidence that the check kept its bound. Nothing the check
0022| # started outlives it: the dedicated group, and the descendants that left it,
0023| # are stopped on every exit path. The installer then checks that
0024| # ``forgel-code`` resolves to the launcher it just wrote. Re-running replaces
0025| # the installation; running with ``--uninstall`` removes it again.
0026| #
0027| # Installing the client alone is not enough to use it, so the same run also
0028| # makes sure an engine the client supports is in place. It asks the engine's own
0029| # installer which version the configured engine source provides, without
0030| # installing anything, and reads the version of an engine that is already
0031| # present. Only then does it decide: an available engine is installed when none
0032| # is present, the present engine is kept when the available one is not newer and
0033| # the present one is supported, a strictly newer available engine replaces the
0034| # present one, and anything else ends the run as a failure that names the
0035| # required minimum, the version found and the action the user can take. A
0036| # successful run always states the engine version in place and how it was
0037| # obtained. ``--client-only`` installs the client alone and touches no engine.
0038| # Reading a version report, and installing a version, are the engine installer's
0039| # own jobs; this script only decides and delegates.
0040| #
0041| # Environment variables:
0042| #   FORGEL_CODE_HOME            install prefix (default: $HOME/.local/share/forgel-code)
0043| #   FORGEL_CODE_BIN             launcher directory (default: $HOME/.local/bin)
0044| #   FORGEL_CODE_SOURCE          local checkout to install from, without network
0045| #   FORGEL_CODE_TAG             repository tag when no checkout is given (default: v0.2.0)
0046| #   FORGEL_CODE_REPOSITORY      repository URL used with FORGEL_CODE_TAG
0047| #   FORGEL_CODE_PYTHON          Python 3 interpreter (default: python3 on PATH)
0048| #   FORGEL_CODE_PROFILE         shell profile to edit (default: chosen from the login shell)
0049| #   FORGEL_CODE_NO_MODIFY_PATH  set to leave the shell profile untouched
0050| #   FORGEL_CODE_NO_PROFILE_EDIT the same opt-out under its older name
0051| #   FORGEL_CODE_TIMEOUT         seconds the fresh-shell check may take (default: 10)
0052| #   FORGEL_ENGINE_SOURCE        engine source the engine installer resolves against
0053| #                               (default: https://github.com/forgel-dev/forgel)
0054| #   FORGEL_ENGINE_INSTALLER     the engine's own installer (default: forgel-install on PATH)
0055| #   FORGEL_ENGINE               engine binary whose version is read (default: forgel on PATH)
0056| #
0057| # The script is POSIX ``sh`` and safe to pipe into: it never reads stdin.
0058|

0125| # What the bounded check owns while it runs: its private directory, the command

0143| # How two engine versions are ordered. The ordering is numeric component by
0144| # component, ignores one leading version marker and trailing zero components, so
0145| # ``v0.2.0``, ``0.2`` and ``0.2.0.0`` are the same version. A version with a
0146| # component that is not a number cannot be ordered at all: the helper exits with
0147| # status 2 and the caller treats that version as not satisfying a minimum.
0148| # ``ge`` and ``gt`` compare; both exit 0 only for a true answer.
0149| VERSION_HELPER='
0150| import sys
0151| 
0152| def parse(text):
0153|     text = text.strip()
0154|     if text[:1] in ("v", "V"):
0155|         text = text[1:]
0156|     if not text:
0157|         return None
0158|     numbers = []
0159|     for part in text.split("."):
0160|         if not part.isdigit() or not part.isascii():
0161|             return None
0162|         numbers.append(int(part))
0163|     while len(numbers) > 1 and numbers[-1] == 0:
0164|         numbers.pop()
0165|     return numbers
0166| 
0167| if len(sys.argv) < 4:
0168|     sys.exit(2)
0169| operator, left, right = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
0170| first = parse(left)
0171| second = parse(right)
0172| if first is None or second is None:
0173|     sys.exit(2)
0174| width = max(len(first), len(second))
0175| first = first + [0] * (width - len(first))
0176| second = second + [0] * (width - len(second))
0177| if operator == "ge":
0178|     sys.exit(0 if first >= second else 1)
0179| if operator == "gt":
0180|     sys.exit(0 if first > second else 1)
0181| sys.exit(2)

0562| # The current time in milliseconds, so the check can be timed. A ``date`` with
0563| # nanoseconds answers with them; one without that extension (macOS writes the
0564| # literal ``N``) falls back to the interpreter the installer already requires,
0565| # and to whole seconds only when nothing finer answers. A host with no usable
0566| # clock reports 0, and the verdict is then the recorded timeout alone.
0567| now_millis() {

0569|     case $stamp in
0570|         ''|*[!0-9]*) stamp= ;;

0572|     if [ "${#stamp}" -ge 19 ]; then
0573|         printf '%s\n' "$((stamp / 1000000))"

0575|     fi

0577|         stamp=$("$PYTHON" -c 'import time; print(int(time.time() * 1000))' 2>/dev/null) || stamp=
0578|         case $stamp in
0579|             ''|*[!0-9]*) stamp= ;;
0580|         esac
0581|         if [ -n "$stamp" ]; then
0582|             printf '%s\n' "$stamp"
0583|             return 0
0584|         fi
0585|     fi
0586|     stamp=$(date +%s 2>/dev/null) || stamp=
0587|     case $stamp in
0588|         ''|*[!0-9]*) stamp=0 ;;
0589|     esac
0590|     printf '%s\n' "$((stamp * 1000))"
0591| }

0635| process_tree() {

0637|         { parent[$1] = $2; ids[NR] = $1 }
0638|         END {
0639|             frontier[0] = root
0640|             count = 1
0641|             for (i = 0; i < count; i++) {
0642|                 for (j = 1; j <= NR; j++) {
0643|                     pid = ids[j]
0644|                     if (parent[pid] == frontier[i] && !(pid in seen)) {
0645|                         seen[pid] = 1
0646|                         frontier[count] = pid
0647|                         count++
0648|                     }
0649|                 }
0650|             }
0651|             for (i = 1; i < count; i++) print frontier[i]
0652|         }'

0655| # Start the checked command in a process group of its own, and record that group
0656| # for the whole lifetime of the check: the command may exit at once while
0657| # something it started lives on in the same group. The launcher puts itself in a
0658| # new session, and so in a new process group, before it runs the command; the
0659| # group id is therefore its own pid. Python is already required to install the
0660| # client. A shell without it falls back to its own job control, and otherwise to
0661| # the descendant sweep alone.
0662| start_check() {
0663|     out=$1
0664|     shift
0665|     if [ -n "${PYTHON:-}" ] && "$PYTHON" -c 'import os' >/dev/null 2>&1; then
0666|         "$PYTHON" -c '
0667| import os, sys
0668| try:
0669|     os.setsid()
0670| except OSError:
0671|     try:
0672|         os.setpgid(0, 0)
0673|     except OSError:
0674|         pass
0675| try:
0676|     os.execvp(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[1:])
0677| except OSError:
0678|     os._exit(127)

0680|     else
0681|         set -m 2>/dev/null || true
0682|         "$@" > "$out" 2>/dev/null < /dev/null &
0683|     fi

0685|     set +m 2>/dev/null || true
0686|     CHECK_GROUP=$CHECK_CHILD

0688| }

0690| # Signal every member of a process group. The caller's own group is never
0691| # signalled, so a check that could not be placed in a group of its own cannot
0692| # make the cleanup reach the installer itself.
0693| signal_group() {
0694|     signal=$1
0695|     group=$2
0696|     case $group in
0697|         ''|*[!0-9]*) return 0 ;;
0698|     esac
0699|     own=
0700|     if command -v ps >/dev/null 2>&1; then
0701|         own=$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ') || own=
0702|     fi
0703|     if [ -n "$own" ] && [ "$group" = "$own" ]; then
0704|         return 0
0705|     fi
0706|     if kill -"$signal" "-$group" 2>/dev/null; then
0707|         return 0
0708|     fi
0709|     # A shell that cannot name a group signals its members one by one.
0710|     for pid in $(process_group "$group"); do
0711|         kill -"$signal" "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true
0712|     done
0713|     return 0
0714| }

0716| # Stop what the checked command started. The dedicated process group is the
0717| # primary target: everything that stayed in it goes at once, on the success path
0718| # as well as on the timeout path. A sweep of the checked command's descendants
0719| # follows, so a descendant that left the group is reached as well.
0720| stop_check() {
0721|     signal=$1
0722|     signal_group "$signal" "$CHECK_GROUP"
0723|     if [ -n "$CHECK_CHILD" ]; then
0724|         for pid in $(process_tree "$CHECK_CHILD"); do
0725|             kill -"$signal" "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true
0726|         done
0727|         kill -"$signal" "$CHECK_CHILD" 2>/dev/null || true
0728|     fi
0729|     return 0
0730| }

0732| # Release everything the bounded check owns: the watchdog, the checked process
0733| # group with the descendants that left it, and the private directory. It runs at
0734| # most once per check, so the exit trap and a signal trap cannot release the
0735| # same check twice and a second call is a no-op. Every piece of state the
0736| # release reads is cleared only after it has been used.
0737| cleanup_check() {
0738|     if [ -n "$CHECK_CLEANED" ]; then
0739|         return 0
0740|     fi
0741|     CHECK_CLEANED=1
0742|     if [ -n "$CHECK_WATCHER" ]; then
0743|         kill -TERM "$CHECK_WATCHER" 2>/dev/null || true
0744|         wait "$CHECK_WATCHER" 2>/dev/null || true
0745|         CHECK_WATCHER=
0746|     fi
0747|     if [ -n "$CHECK_GROUP" ] || [ -n "$CHECK_CHILD" ]; then
0748|         stop_check KILL
0749|         if [ -n "$CHECK_CHILD" ]; then
0750|             wait "$CHECK_CHILD" 2>/dev/null || true
0751|         fi
0752|         CHECK_GROUP=
0753|         CHECK_CHILD=
0754|     fi
0755|     if [ -n "$CHECK_DIR" ]; then
0756|         rm -rf "$CHECK_DIR" 2>/dev/null || true
0757|         CHECK_DIR=
0758|     fi
0759|     return 0
0760| }

0767| # Wait, for a bounded moment, until the watchdog has recorded its decision in
0768| # the private check directory: ``timed-out`` when the bound had elapsed before
0769| # the checked command exited, ``finished`` when it saw the command gone first.
0770| # Status 0 means the decision is there, 1 that the watchdog did not answer
0771| # within DECISION_WAIT seconds. The decision says which stop to expect; it is
0772| # not the verdict, which is the time the check took (see ``bounded_run``). The
0773| # wait never depends on the checked command, so a watchdog that never answers
0774| # delays the installer by that fixed limit at most.
0775| await_decision() {
0776|     decision_dir=$1
0777|     waited=0
0778|     while :; do
0779|         if [ -e "$decision_dir/timed-out" ] || [ -e "$decision_dir/finished" ]; then
0780|             return 0
0781|         fi
0782|         if [ "$waited" -ge "$DECISION_WAIT" ]; then
0783|             return 1
0784|         fi
0785|         sleep 1 2>/dev/null || true
0786|         waited=$((waited + 1))
0787|     done
0788| }

0790| # Run a command under a hard time bound. ``timeout`` from GNU coreutils is not
0791| # required and is not used: the command runs in the background and a watchdog
0792| # stops it once the bound elapsed. The watchdog records ``timed-out`` in the
0793| # private directory before it starts the graceful stop, and ``finished`` when it
0794| # saw the command gone before the bound; that record says which stop to expect,
0795| # never what the verdict is. The installer times the check itself and reports a
0796| # timeout whenever the measured time reached the bound, so the ordering between
0797| # the command's own exit, the record and the read of the result cannot turn a
0798| # step that overran into a success. A command that finished inside the bound
0799| # keeps its own status, a nonzero one included. After the graceful stop the
0800| # watchdog forcefully stops the rest of the checked command's process group once
0801| # the grace period has passed. Nothing the function starts survives it.
0802| # CHECK_STATUS is 124 when the bound elapsed.
0803| #
0804| # The checked command leads a process group of its own (see ``start_check``), so
0805| # the group is what the cleanup signals, on the success path as much as on the
0806| # timeout path. Its three standard descriptors are redirected, so the group has
0807| # no terminal to hold it and cannot stop on a terminal access.
0808| bounded_run() {
0809|     limit=$1
0810|     shift
0811|     CHECK_STATUS=0
0812|     CHECK_OUTPUT=
0813|     CHECK_CLEANED=
0814|     CHECK_CHILD=
0815|     CHECK_GROUP=
0816|     if ! create_check_dir; then
0817|         return 1
0818|     fi
0819|     out=$CHECK_DIR/output
0820|     timed_out=$CHECK_DIR/timed-out
0821|     finished=$CHECK_DIR/finished
0822|     saved_umask=$(umask)
0823|     umask 077
0824|     if ! : > "$out"; then
0825|         umask "$saved_umask"
0826|         cleanup_check
0827|         return 1
0828|     fi
0829|     started=$(now_millis)
0830|     start_check "$out" "$@"
0831|     umask "$saved_umask"
0832|     child=$CHECK_CHILD
0833|     (
0834|         exec > /dev/null 2>&1 < /dev/null
0835|         sleeper=
0836|         trap 'kill "$sleeper" 2>/dev/null || true; exit 0' TERM
0837|         elapsed=0
0838|         while [ "$elapsed" -lt "$limit" ]; do
0839|             sleep 1 &
0840|             sleeper=$!
0841|             wait "$sleeper" 2>/dev/null || true
0842|             sleeper=
0843|             elapsed=$((elapsed + 1))
0844|             if ! kill -0 "$child" 2>/dev/null; then
0845|                 # The command was gone inside the bound; record that so the
0846|                 # caller knows which stop to expect.
0847|                 : > "$finished" 2>/dev/null || true
0848|                 exit 0
0849|             fi
0850|         done
0851|         : > "$timed_out" 2>/dev/null || true
0852|         stop_check TERM
0853|         sleep "$VERIFY_GRACE" 2>/dev/null || true
0854|         stop_check KILL
0855|     ) &
0856|     CHECK_WATCHER=$!
0857|     wait "$child" || CHECK_STATUS=$?
0858|     ended=$(now_millis)
0859|     measured=$((ended - started))
0860|     if await_decision "$CHECK_DIR"; then
0861|         # The watchdog records its decision before it stops anything, so on
0862|         # the timeout path it may still own the graceful then the forceful
0863|         # stop; let it finish so nothing outlives the check.
0864|         wait "$CHECK_WATCHER" 2>/dev/null || true
0865|     else
0866|         # A watchdog that never answers is not allowed to hold the installer. A
0867|         # decision that never arrives is not evidence that the bound was kept;
0868|         # the measured time decides that below.
0869|         kill -KILL "$CHECK_WATCHER" 2>/dev/null || true
0870|         wait "$CHECK_WATCHER" 2>/dev/null || true
0871|     fi
0872|     # The verdict is the time the check took, never the presence of a record: a
0873|     # step that outlived the bound is a timeout even when it exited on its own
0874|     # before the timeout was recorded, and a step inside the bound keeps its own
0875|     # status, a nonzero one included.
0876|     if [ -e "$timed_out" ] || [ "$measured" -ge "$((limit * 1000))" ]; then
0877|         CHECK_STATUS=124
0878|     fi
0879|     CHECK_OUTPUT=$(cat "$out") || CHECK_OUTPUT=
0880|     # The check is released here, before any state the release reads is
0881|     # cleared: a successful check leaves nothing behind, exactly like a failed
0882|     # or a timed-out one.
0883|     cleanup_check
0884|     return 0
0885| }

Forgel Code — thin console client for Forgel over the engine's machine-readable
commands.

The client does not import the engine. Its only channel is running
`forgel <command> --json` as a separate process and reading exactly one JSON
object from stdout. The model, sandbox, independent QA, review and release
approval stay in the engine: the client never calls a model, never reads
project files and never runs checks itself.

## Install

Forgel Code installs with one command. It needs Python 3.9 or newer with the
`pip` module it ships, and the `forgel` engine on `PATH`.

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forgel-dev/code/v0.2.0/install.sh | sh
```

The installer puts the client into `~/.local/share/forgel-code` and a
`forgel-code` launcher into `~/.local/bin`, then adds that directory to `PATH`
through one marked block in the profile your login shell reads. No virtual
environment and no activation step are involved, and the same command run again
replaces the installation instead of duplicating anything.

| Login shell | Profile file that receives the block |
| --- | --- |
| zsh | `~/.zshrc` |
| bash | the first existing of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.profile`; `~/.bash_profile` is created when none of them exists |
| other POSIX `sh` | `~/.profile`, with a warning on stderr that names the file and the detected shell |

The login shell comes from `$SHELL`. When that is unset, empty or names a shell
the installer does not handle, it reads the shell of the invoking process and
then the account login shell — the macOS Directory Service entry, otherwise the
passwd entry — and only then falls back to `~/.profile`. The block is never
written to `~/.bashrc` alone, because a login bash shell does not read that
file. A profile file that does not exist yet is created.

The block carries a `case "$PATH:"` guard and prepends the launcher directory
only when it is not already there, so sourcing it again, or sourcing several
profiles that carry it, leaves exactly one entry. There is no unguarded
`export PATH=...` line.

After writing the block the installer checks it: it starts the detected login
shell as a login interactive shell from a cleared environment, under a bounded
time limit enforced without GNU `timeout`, and requires `command -v forgel-code`
to resolve to the launcher it just wrote. On success it prints the detected
shell, the edited profile file and the path that fresh shell resolved. If the
check fails, or the shell does not answer within the limit, it exits non-zero
and prints on stderr the edited profile file, the exact block it wrote, the
shell it checked, the `PATH` that shell saw and what `forgel-code` resolved to,
so a profile your login shell never reads is never reported as active.
Re-running keeps exactly one marked block and leaves the rest of the file as it
was.

The client has no dependencies and builds through the small in-tree PEP 517
backend (`_build_backend.py`), so the installer never needs a package index.
Editable installs are not supported: the backend implements only the
`build_wheel` and `build_sdist` hooks.

| --- | --- |

## Interactive session

Starting `forgel-code` with no arguments opens an interactive session instead of
printing usage text. It shows a prompt and stays open until you leave, so you
work by writing sentences rather than by translating every intent into a
command.

Each sentence is handed to the engine's project agent as one free-form request
and the agent's answer is shown in the session. The session also shows the
project it is working on, and re-reads the task and release state from the
engine on its own, so progress becomes visible without asking for a status
again.

Some sentences ask the session for one specific action:

| You write | What the session asks the engine for |
| --- | --- |
| a plain sentence | the project agent's answer |
| `plan <goal>` | a plan for the goal, shown with its tasks in plan order and their states |
| `accept <task>` | accepting that task |
| `rework <task> <remarks>` | sending that task back with the remarks |
| `retry <task>` | retrying that task |
| `pause` | pausing work |
| `resume` | resuming work |
| `switch to <key>` | selecting another project; every later request and every later state shown uses the new project |
| `leave`, `exit`, `quit`, or the end of the input | ending the session |

A sentence that names no action, or more than one, gets a clarification and
nothing is carried out. A request that becomes a plan shows its tasks in plan
order, and one that becomes a task shows that task with its title and state.
When an engine call fails, the session shows the reason and the next possible
step and stays usable for the next request; leaving after a failure needs no
restart. Replies follow the language of your message.

Adopting a repository, creating a project, setting or changing a secret and
changing configuration are not part of the conversation. A sentence never
carries them out; the session only points you to the explicit command for them.

Leaving ends the session at once: the client sends nothing further to the
engine and keeps no transcript. Key material never reaches the screen, because
a value that names a secret is replaced before it is shown.

The interactive session adds no capability of its own: every answer and every
piece of state comes from the engine, and the client still calls no model, reads
no project and runs no check. All commands below keep working one-shot, with the
same output, exit status and `--json` form as before.

## Commands

Every client command is a thin wrapper over an existing engine command, and
the engine is always called with `--json`. `<key>` below is the project the
client session selected with `forgel-code use`; while nothing is selected the
client passes no `--project` and the engine keeps its own active project.

| Client command | Engine command | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `forgel-code say <phrase>` | `forgel say "<phrase>"` | Turn a free phrase into a task |
| `forgel-code status` | `forgel status` | State of the task and the milestone |
| `forgel-code tasks` | `forgel tasks` | List tasks |
| `forgel-code task <task>` | `forgel tasks` | State of one task, picked out of the engine's task list |
| `forgel-code accept <task>` | `forgel task accept --task <task> [--project <key>]` | Accept a task |
| `forgel-code rework <task> <remark...>` | `forgel task reject --task <task> --notes "<remark>" [--project <key>]` | Send a task back for rework with remarks |
| `forgel-code resume` | `forgel resume` | Start or resume work |
| `forgel-code pause` | `forgel pause` | Pause work |
| `forgel-code plan "<goal>" [--milestone <key>]` | `forgel plan [<key>] --goal "<goal>"` | Decompose the milestone goal into tasks |
| `forgel-code history` | `forgel history` | Short session history |
| `forgel-code projects` | `forgel projects` | List projects |
| `forgel-code session` | `forgel session` | Show the session the engine reports |
| `forgel-code use <key>` | `forgel use <key>` | Select the active project |

`forgel-code` does not read a project itself: `task <task>` asks the engine for
its task list and shows the one task you named. If that task is not in the
engine's answer — or appears there more than once — the client reports it and
exits with a non-zero code.

`accept` and `rework` lean on the engine's `task` command and its positional
actions: accepting is `task accept`, sending back is `task reject`, and the
remarks travel in the engine's `--notes`. The client adds no subcommand and no
option of its own. The exact engine calls behind them are:

```sh
forgel task accept --task <task> --json
forgel task reject --task <task> --notes "<remark>" --json
```

When the running engine does not provide the action a point needs, the client
prints the engine's own message plus an explicit note ("no engine command for
this point") and exits with a non-zero code instead of inventing behaviour.
That decision is taken from the engine's return code and structured error
fields, never from the wording of its message, so it does not depend on the
locale.

### Output

Without a flag a command prints human readable text. With `--json` it prints
exactly one JSON object to stdout:

```json
{"command": "status", "project": "acme", "ok": true, "result": {}}
```

The `project` field is the project key actually handed to the engine, or `null`
when nothing was passed. On failure — including an argument-parse error — the
client exits with a non-zero code and, with `--json`, prints one JSON object
with `"ok": false` and the message under `error`. A structured engine refusal
(`"ok": false` in the engine's answer) is a failure even when the engine exits
with code 0, and its own fields are carried through. A failure report names the
engine that answered: the path configured by `--engine`, `$FORGEL_ENGINE` or
`forgel` leads the message.

### Active project

`forgel-code use <key>` hands the key to the engine and, only when the engine
accepts it, makes it the active project; every project-scoped command then
passes `--project <key>`. `forgel-code projects` lists what the engine knows
about. Until you pick a key no `--project` argument is sent, so the engine's own
active project is used. Set `FORGEL_CODE_HOME` to move the session file.

### Timeout

The engine call is bounded. `--timeout SECONDS` sets the limit for one call,
`$FORGEL_CODE_TIMEOUT` sets it for the environment, and the default is 600
seconds. When the limit elapses the client kills the engine and fails with a
structured error instead of blocking. The engine's stdout is always decoded as
UTF-8 and the child process does not receive the client's stdin.

`--json`, `--engine` and `--timeout` are parsed as options of their own and are
never substituted inside argument text, so a phrase or remark that mentions
such a word reaches the engine unchanged. Put `--` before a remark that itself
begins with a hyphen.

## Tests

From a checkout the suite needs nothing but the Python standard library and no
network access:

```sh
python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

That command runs the whole suite — no environment variable, marker or default
option leaves a test out — and it covers the installer scenarios too, which run
the real `install.sh` with a real install through `pip` into a temporary home
directory and a real detected login shell.

Installing the client with its `test` extra brings the pytest the wheel
declares, so a pinned revision can run the same suite too:

```sh
python3 -m pip install "https://github.com/forgel-dev/code/archive/refs/tags/v0.1.1.tar.gz[test]"
python -m pytest -q
```

Leaving ends the session at once: the client sends nothing further to the
engine and keeps no transcript. Key material never reaches the screen, because
a value that names a secret is replaced before it is shown.

The interactive session adds no capability of its own: every answer and every
piece of state comes from the engine, and the client still calls no model, reads
no project and runs no check. All commands below keep working one-shot, with the
same output, exit status and `--json` form as before.

## Commands

Every client command is a thin wrapper over an existing engine command, and
the engine is always called with `--json`. `<key>` below is the project the
client session selected with `forgel-code use`; while nothing is selected the
client passes no `--project` and the engine keeps its own active project.

| Client command | Engine command | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `forgel-code say <phrase>` | `forgel say "<phrase>"` | Turn a free phrase into a task |
| `forgel-code status` | `forgel status` | State of the task and the milestone |
| `forgel-code tasks` | `forgel tasks` | List tasks |
| `forgel-code task <task>` | `forgel tasks` | State of one task, picked out of the engine's task list |
| `forgel-code accept <task>` | `forgel task accept --task <task> [--project <key>]` | Accept a task |
| `forgel-code rework <task> <remark...>` | `forgel task reject --task <task> --notes "<remark>" [--project <key>]` | Send a task back for rework with remarks |
| `forgel-code resume` | `forgel resume` | Start or resume work |
| `forgel-code pause` | `forgel pause` | Pause work |
| `forgel-code plan "<goal>" [--milestone <key>]` | `forgel plan [<key>] --goal "<goal>"` | Decompose the milestone goal into tasks |
| `forgel-code history` | `forgel history` | Short session history |
| `forgel-code projects` | `forgel projects` | List projects |
| `forgel-code session` | `forgel session` | Show the session the engine reports |
| `forgel-code use <key>` | `forgel use <key>` | Select the active project |

`forgel-code` does not read a project itself: `task <task>` asks the engine for
its task list and shows the one task you named. If that task is not in the
engine's answer — or appears there more than once — the client reports it and
exits with a non-zero code.

`accept` and `rework` lean on the engine's `task` command and its positional
actions: accepting is `task accept`, sending back is `task reject`, and the
remarks travel in the engine's `--notes`. The client adds no subcommand and no
option of its own. The exact engine calls behind them are:

```sh
forgel task accept --task <task> --json
forgel task reject --task <task> --notes "<remark>" --json
```

When the running engine does not provide the action a point needs, the client
prints the engine's own message plus an explicit note ("no engine command for
this point") and exits with a non-zero code instead of inventing behaviour.
That decision is taken from the engine's return code and structured error
fields, never from the wording of its message, so it does not depend on the
locale.

### Output

Without a flag a command prints human readable text. With `--json` it prints
exactly one JSON object to stdout:

```json
{"command": "status", "project": "acme", "ok": true, "result": {}}
```

The `project` field is the project key actually handed to the engine, or `null`
when nothing was passed. On failure — including an argument-parse error — the
client exits with a non-zero code and, with `--json`, prints one JSON object
with `"ok": false` and the message under `error`. A structured engine refusal
(`"ok": false` in the engine's answer) is a failure even when the engine exits
with code 0, and its own fields are carried through. A failure report names the
engine that answered: the path configured by `--engine`, `$FORGEL_ENGINE` or
`forgel` leads the message.

### Active project

`forgel-code use <key>` hands the key to the engine and, only when the engine
accepts it, makes it the active project; every project-scoped command then
passes `--project <key>`. `forgel-code projects` lists what the engine knows
about. Until you pick a key no `--project` argument is sent, so the engine's own
active project is used. Set `FORGEL_CODE_HOME` to move the session file.

### Timeout

The engine call is bounded. `--timeout SECONDS` sets the limit for one call,
`$FORGEL_CODE_TIMEOUT` sets it for the environment, and the default is 600
seconds. When the limit elapses the client kills the engine and fails with a
structured error instead of blocking. The engine's stdout is always decoded as
UTF-8 and the child process does not receive the client's stdin.

`--json`, `--engine` and `--timeout` are parsed as options of their own and are
never substituted inside argument text, so a phrase or remark that mentions
such a word reaches the engine unchanged. Put `--` before a remark that itself
begins with a hyphen.

## Tests

From a checkout the suite needs nothing but the Python standard library and no
network access:

```sh
python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

That command runs the whole suite — no environment variable, marker or default
option leaves a test out — and it covers the installer scenarios too, which run
the real `install.sh` with a real install through `pip` into a temporary home
directory and a real detected login shell.

Installing the client with its `test` extra brings the pytest the wheel
declares, so a pinned revision can run the same suite too:

```sh
python3 -m pip install "https://github.com/forgel-dev/code/archive/refs/tags/v0.1.1.tar.gz[test]"
python -m pytest -q
```
